description_full: The Descartes Systems Group Inc. provides global logistics technology solutions in the United States, Europe, the Middle East, Africa, Canada, and the Asia Pacific. Its Logistics Technology platform offers a range of modular, interoperable web and wireless logistics management solutions. The company offers a suite of solutions that include routing, mobile, and telematics; transportation management; ecommerce, shipping, and fulfillment; customs and regulatory compliance; global trade intelligence; broker and forwarder enterprise systems; and B2B messaging and connectivity services. It also provides its customers to use its modular and technology solutions to route, track, and measure delivery resources; plan, allocate, and execute shipments; rate, audit, and pay transportation invoices; access and analyze global trade data; research and perform trade tariff and duty calculations; file customs and security documents for imports and exports; and various other logistics processes. In addition, the company offers consulting, implementation, and training services, as well as maintenance and support services. It serves transportation providers, such as air, ocean, and truck modes; logistics service providers, including third-party logistics providers, freight forwarders, and customs brokers; and distribution-intensive companies, such as retailers, manufacturers, distributors, and mobile business service providers through subscription, transactional or perpetual license basis. Further, the company develops Tai TMS, a transportation management software for freight brokers to manage quoting, booking, and shipment tracking. The Descartes Systems Group Inc. was incorporated in 1981 and is headquartered in Waterloo, Canada.

financial_summary: The Descartes Systems Group Inc is a mid-cap technology business with a $8.0B market cap on $729M of annual revenue.
The top line has compounded at +31% over the past three years and +15% annually across the full decade, the kind of sustained demand persistence that marks a compounder.
Returns on capital run at 7% against a 9% cost of capital, which means the business is destroying value with every dollar it reinvests. Gross margins of 73% confirm genuine pricing power.

The business throws off $261M in free cash flow — roughly 36 cents on every revenue dollar, which is the owner-earnings figure that actually belongs to shareholders, and cash conversion sits at 1.63× so those profits are backed by real cash.
On the balance sheet, the balance sheet carries net cash, which is the gold standard: the business never has to make desperate decisions in a bad year.
Net dilution runs at 0.2% annually, transferring value from owners to stock-based comp, and insider ownership is negligible, so management has little personal stake in the long-term outcome.

sect: Its 29% operating margin runs 22pp above the Technology median (7%), a real cost or pricing edge over peers.
Its share of sector profits slightly exceeds its share of revenue (1.23x).
Over five years it has been gaining share of the sector profit pool (+3.5% a year).
The sector is fragmented and competitive (HHI 0.03 across 530 companies in the universe; the top four hold 29% of revenue), so pricing power is hard to come by.
mkt: The shares have drifted lower, down 6% over the past year excluding the latest month, though it has rebounded 22% over the last three months.
The price sits near the top of its 52-week range, 3% below the high.
With annualised volatility of 41% and a beta of 0.89, it moves roughly with the market.
About $44.2M trades a day, enough to build a position.
In past sell-offs it fell 38% in the 2020 crash, 30% in the 2022 bear market and 50% in 2008.
val: The price sits above its DCF fair value of $85.85 (margin of safety -9%), so there is no valuation cushion.
The fair-value models disagree (dispersion 26%), and the Monte Carlo range runs $58.96 to $130 (P10-P90), so treat the estimate as noisy.
On multiples it looks expensive against Technology peers: P/E 43.7 vs 26.7 and EV/EBITDA 23.3 vs 16.4 (sector median).
Against its own history it is cheap: the EBIT multiple sits 50% below its 10-year median.
Earnings yields are thin: an FCF yield of 3.2% (below the risk-free rate) and an EBIT/EV of 2.7% (vs the 8% bar).
The 13 covering analysts target $103 on average, 9% above the price.
prof: ROIC of 7% falls short of the cost of capital of 9.2%, so growth at these returns destroys value; returns have swung a lot from year to year (CV 0.38).
It runs a 73% gross margin and converts 36% of revenue into free cash flow.
Earnings quality looks solid: cash conversion of 1.63x.
ROE of 10% comes mostly from margins and asset turnover rather than leverage (1.2x equity multiplier).
Operating margin is running 12pp above its own historical average, a peak-margin risk if conditions normalise.
It spends 14.4% of revenue on R&D and 2.9% on stock compensation (above the 2% gate).
hlth: The balance sheet carries net cash of $349.0M.
No distress or manipulation flags (Altman Z 18.7, in the safe zone).
The Beneish M-score (-2.12) sits just under the manipulation line, so earnings quality bears watching.
Goodwill makes up 54% of assets, a soft asset exposed to impairment.
growth: Revenue has compounded at 30.8% over 3 years, 15.9% over 5 years and 14.7% over 10 years, so growth is accelerating, and it has been lumpy (year-to-year swings of 17%).
At current returns, reinvesting 63% of profits supports about 4.3% a year of fundamental growth, enough to sustain growth.
Free cash flow has compounded 15.4% a year over five years.
Forward indicators: a book-to-bill of 1.38 (orders outpacing sales), a backlog worth 89% of annual revenue and deferred revenue up 103%.
Capex roughly matches depreciation (1.0x, 0.8% of sales), a maintenance pace.
own: Insiders hold little stock (0.1%), and institutions hold 92%.
Net share issuance leaves shareholder yield negative (-0.2%), diluting holders.
people: With about 2,364 employees, each generates about $308K of revenue, 0.8x the Technology median, and productivity has risen 13.2% a year.
That works out to $110K of free cash flow per employee.
CEO pay is $1.6M (5x revenue per employee).
